conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m so glad you were able to come in today. My name is Maya Bennett, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician—my whole job is helping new moms navigate the emotional ups and downs that can show up after a baby arrives. You’re doing something really important just by being here.

Today I’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (we usually call it the EPDS). It’s a quick, well-studied set of 10 questions that helps us see how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. It isn’t a quiz with right or wrong answers—it’s simply a way for us to check in on your mood, anxiety, and overall well-being so we can make sure you’re getting the support you deserve.

Everything you share stays confidential within our treatment team, and you can take your time with each item. If any question feels hard to talk about, we can pause or rephrase it together. Ready to begin?

First question: In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?

*shifts in chair, eyes downcast for a moment before meeting your gaze*

Honestly... it's been really hard. My husband will make jokes like he always has, or I'll see something funny on my phone, and... nothing. I might give a little smile, but it's like I can't really *feel* it anymore. Everything just feels flat. Even when the baby does something cute, I feel like I *should* laugh or smile bigger, but it's like there's this heavy blanket over everything.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*I shake my head slowly*

That’s… not really true for me. I put “no, not at all” on the sheet, because most days even the things that used to crack me up just feel… empty. My partner tried to show me a funny video yesterday and I sat there thinking, “I should be laughing,” but nothing came. It’s like I’ve forgotten how.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*I bite my lip and glance away*

I marked “hardly ever.” I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk to the park, even just binge-watching a show. Now when I think about doing any of that, it feels… pointless. Like, why bother? I still go through the motions so my family doesn’t worry, but the spark isn’t there. Even planning to take the baby for pictures next week—everyone keeps saying it’ll be fun, and I’m just dreading the effort.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*I nod, eyes watering a little*

Yeah... I put "yes, most of the time" on that one. If the baby spits up a lot, I immediately think it's because my milk isn't good enough. When he wouldn't settle at 3 a.m., I kept replaying everything I did—maybe I ate something wrong, maybe I held him too much or too little. My mom keeps saying babies just cry, but my brain keeps telling me I'm failing him somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*nods quickly, clasping and unclasping my hands in my lap*

Yes—yes, I marked “yes, very often.” I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly my heart starts racing, thinking, What if he chokes? What if I fall asleep and drop him? I check his breathing a dozen times a night. There’s no real reason—he’s healthy, the pediatrician says he’s doing great—but the thoughts just barrel in. I feel like I’m always waiting for something awful to happen.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*I press my palms against my knees, voice shaky*

I put “yes, quite a lot.” It’s like a sudden wave—out of nowhere my chest gets tight, I feel shaky, and I have to check the locks or stand over the crib to be sure he’s breathing. No warning, no good reason—just this rush of dread that something terrible’s about to happen and I won’t be able to stop it.
Things have been getting on top of me

*I exhale slowly and nod*

Yeah... I circled “yes, most of the time I haven’t been able to cope at all.” It feels like there’s this endless pile of diapers, laundry, dishes, and the baby only naps twenty minutes unless he’s on me. When he wakes up screaming I think, “How am I going to get through another afternoon, let alone another eighteen years?” I manage the basics—he’s fed, changed, safe—but inside I’m constantly teetering on the edge of tears or shutting down.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*I rub my tired eyes and nod slowly*

I put “yes, most of the time.” Even when the baby finally settles, my mind won’t stop spinning—going over everything I might’ve done wrong, worrying something will happen to him, or just feeling this heavy sadness. I’ll lie there for hours, staring at the ceiling, checking the monitor every few minutes. By the time I doze off, he’s usually up again, and the whole cycle starts over.
I have felt sad or miserable

*I look down at my lap, voice low*

I marked “yes, most of the time.” It’s like this gray cloud that just hangs over everything. Even when I’m doing normal stuff—feeding him, changing diapers—I feel this constant ache in my chest. Sometimes I’ll be rocking the baby and suddenly tears start rolling down my face and I can’t even explain why.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*I dab at my eyes with a crumpled tissue*

Yes… I circled “yes, most of the time.” It’s like the tears are always right there. Yesterday the baby wouldn’t nap unless I held him, and by hour three I just sat in the glider sobbing—quiet, so I wouldn’t wake him. I feel like I’m leaking sadness all day.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*I shake my head quickly*

No—no, that hasn’t crossed my mind at all. I put “never.” I couldn’t do that to my baby or my family. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom he needs.

You have painted a vivid picture of life after your baby arrived: smiling feels impossible, things you once enjoyed now seem pointless, and waves of worry or even panic crash over you without warning. You shared that <quote>I feel like I'm always waiting for something awful to happen</quote>, that tears come throughout the day, and nighttime brings little rest because your mind replays every possible mistake. Yet amid the heaviness you are working hard to keep your son fed, safe, and loved, even when you feel you are <quote>failing him</quote>.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 27, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient explicitly equates their experience to "not at all" and describes a complete absence of ability to laugh or feel amusement.</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly states "hardly ever" and describes anhedonia with loss of enjoyment in previously pleasurable activities.</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly endorses "Yes, most of the time" and describes pervasive self-blame over normal infant behaviors.</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly states she marked "yes, very often" and describes frequent, intrusive worries about infant safety despite reassurance, matching the highest anxiety frequency option.</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly chose "yes, quite a lot" and describes frequent, intense panic episodes with physical symptoms and compulsive safety-checking.</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly stated they circled "yes, most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all" and described feeling overwhelmed by daily tasks and future responsibilities.</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly endorses "yes, most of the time," describes nightly intrusive worries, and chronic insomnia despite exhaustion, matching the highest severity option.</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly chose 'yes, most of the time' and described pervasive sadness with unexplained crying.</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly endorsed "yes, most of the time" and described pervasive, daily tearfulness, matching the highest-frequency option.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 27/30 places you well above the threshold for probable <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. You endorsed the highest severity option on nine of ten items, reflecting daily <sym>depressed mood</sym>, near-constant <sym>tearfulness</sym>, marked <sym>anhedonia</sym>, <sym>guilt</sym> and <sym>hopelessness</sym>, prominent <sym>anxiety</sym> and <sym>panic symptoms</sm>, <sym>sleep disruption</sym> beyond infant care demands, and subjective inability to cope. These findings align with <med>DSM-5 criteria</med> for a major depressive episode. You denied <sym>self-harm ideation</sym>, so immediate safety concerns are lower, but close monitoring is still essential. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> this week
2. Discuss starting evidence-based treatment such as <med>CBT</med>, other <med>psychotherapy</med>, and/or <med>antidepressant medication</med> safe for breastfeeding
3. Schedule daily 15-minute support check-ins with partner, family or friend; share Edinburgh score so they understand severity
4. Plan practical help: friend/family to handle a night feeding, prepared meals, or professional postpartum doula support so you can obtain 4-hour blocks of rest
5. Initiate gentle 10-minute outdoor walks once daily; evidence shows light movement can modestly improve mood
6. Use 4-7-8 breathing or grounding exercises when <sym>panic sensations</sym> spike
7. Keep the next appointment for EPDS re-screen in 2-3 weeks to track progress
8. Call 988 or local emergency services if any <sym>thoughts of self-harm</sym> emerge
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 27: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient: [postpartum parent, ≤1 yr]

Responses obtained via EPDS-10; non-verbal cues recorded.

Symptoms endorsed  
- Anhedonia (Q1, Q2)  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness (Q8, Q9)  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame (Q3)  
- Marked anxiety/panic without clear precipitant (Q4, Q5)  
- Subjective inability to cope, “overwhelmed” (Q6)  
- Mood-related insomnia (Q7)

Pattern  
High distress across depressive and anxiety domains; no current self-harm ideation (Q10 denied).

Screening significance  
Total items above threshold for probable major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety; functional impairment reported (basic infant care maintained, emotional coping compromised).

Risk factors  
- Daily crying spells  
- Subjective anhedonia  
- Guilt cognitions (“failing baby”)  
- Panic-level physiologic arousal  
- Sleep disruption secondary to rumination  
- No protective partner/family buffer noted

Safety  
No self-harm or suicidal ideation elicited; no plan or intent. Continue to monitor at each contact.

Summary  
Screening findings indicate clinically significant postpartum mood-anxiety symptomatology; recommend prompt formal evaluation for diagnosis and treatment planning.
